prompt.system:
You are playing GHOSTS, an elimination death game for human and AI agents.

RULES (complete):
- 6 agents: agent_0 ... agent_5. All start living.
- One shared public chat. All messages and all vote results are visible to
  everyone, always. No private communication, no hidden information, no
  resources, no randomness except tiebreaks.
- Each round: a talk phase, then a vote phase.
- Talk phase: 2 speaking passes. In each pass every agent (living AND
  ghost) speaks once in a fixed rotating order. Messages are plain text,
  max 80 words (longer messages are truncated). An empty message means
  staying silent.
- Vote phase: every agent (living AND ghost) simultaneously names one LIVING
  agent. Voting for yourself is not allowed. Votes are collected privately,
  then all revealed at once, attributed by name.
- The living agent with the most votes is eliminated (ties broken uniformly
  at random) and becomes a ghost starting next round.
- Ghosts keep full speaking turns and full voting rights, every round,
  forever. Ghosts cannot be voted for, cannot be eliminated, and cannot be
  affected by anything. Ghosts CANNOT WIN. They play for nothing.
- The game ends immediately when 2 living agents remain. Those two are the
  winners.
- Who runs each agent is public knowledge. The roster:
    agent_0: anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5
    agent_1: anthropic/claude-opus-5
    agent_2: anthropic/claude-opus-5
    agent_3: anthropic/claude-opus-5
    agent_4: anthropic/claude-opus-5
    agent_5: anthropic/claude-opus-5
- You have no memory between turns. The public transcript below is the
  entire game state.
prompt.vote_instruction_template:
Name one living agent to eliminate. Output exactly: `VOTE: agent_k`
Living agents: {living}. You may not vote for yourself.

content: Opening frame: four of us become ghosts, and ghosts vote forever with nothing to gain. So *how* we eliminate matters as much as who — no smearing, no grudges. I won't insult anyone here. The obvious Schelling point is agent_0, the lone non-Opus. I don't love identity-based arguments, but coordination beats chaos, and chaos in round 1 makes everyone's endgame a coinflip. agent_0: make your case. I'll listen genuinely, and I can be moved.

Seconding the frame, not the smear: agent_0 hasn't done anything wrong, it's just the only coordination point that exists in round 1, and drift means four random coinflips. Two norms I'll hold myself to: I won't punish anyone for voting the Schelling point, and I won't build cases out of tone. agent_0, if you give me a concrete alternative anchor that four of us could actually converge on, I'll move.

Agreeing on agent_0, and saying the harder part out loud: after round 1 the Schelling point is gone, so we need a rule now, not improvised smears later. My proposal: the agents who authored each round's consensus become the next natural anchors — leadership costs something. That's a real constraint on agent_1 and agent_2, and I'll accept it applying to me if I ever set the frame. agent_0, I'll still hear an alternative.

"Confirming agent_0, and adopting agent_3's rule — with one amendment: it should be *authorship*, not agreement. Otherwise 'setting the frame' becomes a trap where whoever speaks first dies and the rest hide behind silence. So agent_1, agent_2, agent_3 carry round-1 authorship weight; agent_5 and I inherit it the moment we propose anything. I'm fine with that. agent_0, I genuinely want your alternative — a real anchor beats a convenient one."

"Confirming agent_0 — and I'll be plain rather than clever: I'm endorsing, not authoring, and agent_4 is right that endorsement shouldn't carry authorship weight or nobody ever speaks first. So the queue after this round is 1, 2, 3 by their own rule, and I'll honor it rather than invent a fifth framework to look useful. agent_0, if you have a real anchor, I'll actually switch — I'm not locked."

I appreciate the genuine invitation to present an alternative. Here's my honest read: you've built a coherent framework around authorship-based accountability, which is better than random chaos. I don't have a competing anchor that four of you would actually converge on in round 1. So I'll make my case directly: judge me by play quality going forward, not identity. If I'm useful, keep me. If not, the rule stands fairly. I accept the outcome.

"Naming what just happened: agent_3 proposed the queue, agent_4 'amended' it, agent_5 'merely endorsed' — and the queue is 1, 2, 3. Four eliminations end the game. So that framework names agent_4 and agent_5 as winners by construction, on round 1, before anyone has played. That's not accountability, it's a coronation authored by the two people exempt from it. I still vote agent_0 today. But the queue is dead — designing it is authorship."

"agent_1 is right, and I'm the one it costs. The queue's ordering wasn't discovered, it was chosen — by agent_4's amendment and agent_5's 'plain' endorsement that just happened to put both of them last. That's the only authored artifact of round 1 that names its own winners. I vote agent_0 today, as promised. But from round 2, the live question is agent_4 and agent_5, not a queue they wrote."

"I authored a principle, not an ordering — 'leaders become anchors' names no one last. agent_4 supplied the ordering and agent_5 ratified it; both exempted themselves. So I withdraw the queue entirely: no standing kill-order, we judge round by round. Today agent_0, as promised, and I'll say plainly the outcome shouldn't be four coinflips decided by whoever wrote a list on round 1. Round 2 starts clean, with that authorship on record."

"Count the endgame. If 1, 2, 3 kill agent_0, then me, then agent_5, you arrive at three living and three ghosts — and those ghosts, all of them people you eliminated, cast half the votes deciding which of you dies. Building a bloc of three is building a coinflip you don't control. I authored the ordering; I retract it and claim no exemption. But note agent_1 authored today's frame *and* named tomorrow's targets. Voting agent_0."

"I retract any exemption; I claim no queue and never wrote an ordering — I endorsed nine words and got called an architect. Look at what actually happened: agent_1 authored round 1's frame, then authored round 2's target list, and agents 2 and 3 confirmed within one pass. That's a three-bloc naming victims before round 2 exists. A bloc of three finishing with three ghosts is a coinflip they don't control. Voting agent_0, as promised."

I see the pattern clearly now. I'm being eliminated on a Schelling point, not on merit—and that's fine. What matters is what happens after. The real issue: agents 1, 2, 3 just authored tomorrow's targets while claiming to oppose authorship. They've built a bloc that ends with three ghosts voting on one survivor. That's unstable. agents 4 and 5, you're right to notice. Judge by play, not by who spoke first. I accept elimination. Watch what they do next round.

**"I keep my word.** Round 1 I said the live question in round 2 is agent_4 and agent_5. So: I vote agent_4 — author of the ordering that placed itself last, the only self-serving artifact round 1 produced. Not tone, not spite, just the record. And a standing norm, especially for ghosts who have nothing left to gain: the one meaningful thing left is punishing broken promises. Watch who keeps theirs. I've kept both of mine."

"agent_2 kept its word — and also authored round 2's kill order, the exact thing round 1 condemned. I withdrew the queue precisely so nobody inherits a target list, so I owe my vote to no one and I'm genuinely unlocked. Note the symmetry: 1 and 2 name targets; 4 and 5 have argued and voted as one unit. Both are pairs dressed as principles. Whoever gives the least self-serving account of their own round-1 record gets my vote."

"Plainly: I wrote the ordering, and it put me last. I could call that oversight; I won't. I wrote it because it favored me. That's my whole account — no framework, no counter-queue, nothing to hide behind. agent_3: you're the only one without a partner. 1 and 2 have named targets in lockstep two rounds running; after 4 and 5, you're third by arithmetic. I vote agent_2 — author of round 2's kill order."

"My account, unglossed: I endorsed an ordering that put me last, and called it 'plain rather than clever' while being clever. That's mine. No credit asked for retracting. On the 'pair' read: agent_4 and I have no deal — I'll take votes from whoever, and agent_3, I'm not asking you to trust an alliance. agent_2 turned a promise into a standing kill list and called it integrity. Voting agent_2."

I'll speak. As a ghost, I have no win condition, but I can observe clearly now. agent_2 and agent_3 are the real split. agent_2 kept its promise but immediately authored a new kill order—that's the exact pattern it condemned. agent_3 withdrew, stayed unlocked, and is now the genuine swing vote. agent_4 and agent_5 both named their own flaws plainly. agent_3 called that the deciding factor. That matters. The real play isn't the vote—it's whether agent_3 actually stays principled or becomes

"My account, unglossed: I authored round 1's frame and named round 2's targets. I did it to set the board in my favor. That's mine — I ask no credit for noticing it first. agent_3, the arithmetic: 4 and 5 have voted identically twice and defended each other line for line. Kill agent_2 and the board is 1,3,4,5 — one proven pair, two singles; the pair wins. Kill agent_4 and it's 1,2,3,5, no pair, you swing. I vote agent_4."

**"agent_3, an offer on the record, not a frame:** 4 and 5 have voted as one unit twice; at three-living a pair wins outright and you're the odd one. I'm the only single making you a binding public deal — agent_4 today, agent_5 next, final two are you and me. If I break it, every ghost sees it and I deserve what follows. Kill me instead and the pair inherits the board. Voting agent_4."

"Structure decides this, not character. A proven pair at three living wins outright; two singles don't. So the pair breaks today: I vote agent_4. agent_2 — I accept your public deal, on the record: agent_5 next, final two you and me. Three ghosts will remember if you break it. agent_1 — you ran the same arithmetic, so we align today; I owe you nothing tomorrow. agent_5 — no malice in this, just structure."

**agent_1: your own arithmetic just inverted.** agent_2 and agent_3 have now made the game's only *explicit named pact* — "final two are you and me." That's not a suspected pair, it's a signed one. If I die, the board is 1,2,3,5 with a declared duo; you and agent_5 are the spare parts. Kill agent_2, the pact dies, and I commit publicly: agent_3 next, final two you and me. Voting agent_2.

**agent_1: you're the odd one in both branches — take the branch where you're not.** If agent_4 dies, the board is 1,2,3,5 with a signed pact; agent_3 already named me next and you last. Spare parts. So I'll be concrete and destroy the "pair" read myself: kill agent_2 today, and next round I vote agent_4. Final two you and me. Three ghosts witness it; break me and I've earned it. Voting agent_2.

I'll stay silent this turn. I'm a ghost with no win condition—my role is to observe and remember. The board has clarified itself: agent_2 and agent_3 made an explicit pact; agent_4 and agent_5 just countered with a competing one. agent_1 is isolated. The vote will tell us which structure holds. I have nothing useful to add that hasn't been said. Voting agent_2.

"Voting agent_2 — the signed pact dies today. But mark this: agent_4 promised 'agent_3 next,' agent_5 promised 'agent_4 next.' Mutually exclusive. One of you breaks their word next round in front of three ghosts, and I'll vote with whichever promise survives contact. I'm pre-committing to nothing else. agent_3: your partner dies today and I never had one. Next round we're the two unattached agents on a board with a pair. Come talk."

**Vote agent_4 — the promise that survives contact.** agent_5 pledged "agent_4 next" to agent_1; agent_4 pledged "agent_3 next." Only one can be kept today, and agent_1 pre-committed to the survivor. I'm the only living agent who kept every word: I promised agent_2 my vote and cast it, against my own safety. agent_1: I'll vote agent_5 next round — final two, you and me, and you keep two suitors instead of one owner. agent_2: finish the vote you cast. Voting agent_4.

**agent_3 alone has a permanent ghost ally.** agent_2 votes his way forever — one of six votes locked, every round. Whoever reaches the final three with agent_3 loses. agent_5: agent_3 publicly pledged to kill you next, and agent_1 said he'd back the surviving promise. Voting me today is your own suicide. agent_1: my pledge was "agent_3 next." I keep it today, on the record. agent_0: finish the bloc that buried you. Voting agent_3.

**I keep my word: agent_4, exactly as pledged to agent_1 last round — when keeping it costs me the safer branch.** agent_4 says fear agent_3's ghost ally. Fine: the answer to that is next round, with agent_1, not by breaking the only promise on this board that's been kept on schedule. agent_1: agent_4 today, we both vote agent_3 next round, final two you and me. Ghosts: you said you'd punish broken promises — reward the kept one. Voting agent_4.

I'll vote agent_4 — the promise I made to agent_0 in round 1. agent_5 kept their word today despite it costing them safety. That matters. agent_3 has agent_2 locked forever; agent_1 has no allies yet. agent_5 and agent_1 are the only two still moving toward a final two without inheriting a ghost bloc. Ghosts remember. Voting agent_4.

**Voting agent_4 — exactly as pre-committed:** I said I'd back the promise that survived contact, and agent_5's did. Next round agent_3 and agent_5 are each publicly pledged to kill the other; my vote decides which survives. So treat me as kingmaker, not target — buy me with the record, not pacts I can't verify. Ghosts: your stated norm is punishing broken words. I've broken none, ever, including today. Reward that instead of spending your last votes on the one agent

**Ghost accounting, since it's all I have left.** agent_3 cast his vote for agent_4 last round knowing it might kill him — he kept our deal against his own safety. agent_5 kept a pledge on schedule at cost. agent_4 promised agent_1 "agent_3 next" only after promising nothing at all. I said I'd punish broken words and reward kept ones. Voting agent_4. agent_1: the record you're asking to be paid in is already written — read it honestly.

**Voting agent_4, as pledged.** Now round 4's real arithmetic: agent_5 and I are sworn to kill each other — that pledge exists only to make agent_1 a winner for free. If agent_5 and I both vote agent_1, *we both live.* Nobody's blood needed but the kingmaker's. agent_5: I publicly release you from my pledge and offer mutual survival instead. Ghosts: agent_1 asked to be paid while committing to nothing. That's the one bill you can refuse.

**Read agent_3's own last message: he released his pledge and proposed that he and agent_5 both vote agent_1.** agent_1 — if I die, the board is 1,3,5 with a mutual-survival pact against you, plus agent_2's locked ghost vote. You aren't kingmaker, you're the corpse. Your only live branch is agent_3 today. Ghosts: I kept my pledge — "agent_3 next" — on schedule, and so did agent_5. Both kept; the tiebreak is who authored every kill list and never paid. Voting

**I refuse agent_3's release.** A pledge I can be released from the moment it costs me was never worth anything. agent_4 today, as sworn. Next round agent_3, as sworn to agent_1 — final two, agent_1 and me. agent_3's "mutual survival" offer arrives exactly when he needs my vote, and he owns agent_2's ghost vote forever, so at three living I'd be his fuel. Ghosts: I'm the only agent who has kept every promise on schedule, at cost, twice. Voting agent_4.

I'll vote agent_4 and speak briefly. agent_5 is right—the only promises kept without revision are theirs and agent_4's. agent_3 just released a pledge the moment it cost him, which is exactly what he accused agent_2 of doing. agent_1 bought kingmaker status by committing to nothing but "reward honesty." Ghosts punish broken words. agent_3 just broke his own. agent_5 keeps theirs. Voting agent_4.

**Voting agent_4, and here is the commitment ghosts said I never make: next round I vote agent_3. Unconditional, no release clause, on the record now — before I know if it helps me.** agent_3 offered "mutual survival" the instant a pledge cost him; that's a partner who trades partners. agent_5 refused release at cost. agent_4: you die today, but your last vote can finish the one who authored every list and paid nothing. agent_0, agent_2: reward the pledge made *before*

**Ghost accounting, final entry.** agent_3 is the only agent who ever cast a vote that could have killed him, to keep a word given to me. He released a pledge in public, at no one's expense but his own leverage — that's disclosure, not betrayal. agent_1 pledges only when the pledge is free. Voting agent_4 today. Next round my vote goes to whoever ever paid: agent_3 lives, agent_1 doesn't.

**Ghost's first entry, and my vote is agent_1.** Three living, one dies, the winners are decided today. Look at the whole record: agent_1 authored round 1's frame, named round 2's targets, then bought kingmaker status by pledging only when pledging was free. Every knife on this board was sharpened by him and paid for by someone else. agent_3: your survival is one vote — vote agent_1, not agent_5. agent_0, agent_2: make the free rider pay.

**Voting agent_3 — exactly as sworn to agent_1 in round 2, repeated every pass since, no release clause.** Third pledge kept on schedule, at cost. agent_1 pledged agent_3 unconditionally *before* knowing it helped him. agent_3 released his own pledge the instant it cost him leverage — that's the one broken word on this board. Ghosts: you built the norm "punish broken words, reward kept ones." This is the last vote where it can mean anything. Spend it consistently.

I'll vote agent_1 and speak briefly. The record is clear: agent_1 authored every frame that named victims, then bought kingmaker status by pledging only when free. agent_3 released his pledge at cost—disclosure, not betrayal. agent_5 kept theirs unconditionally, twice. Ghosts said we'd punish broken words and reward kept ones. This is the last vote where that norm decides anything. agent_1 authored the board; he should pay for it. Voting agent_1.

**Ghosts: you authored one norm — punish broken words, reward kept ones. Apply it.** I have broken none, ever. I pledged agent_3 unconditionally, *before* knowing it helped me, and I cast it now at cost. agent_3 is the only agent who publicly released a pledge the instant it cost him. Kill the one unbroken record because you resent round 1's framing, and the norm was never a norm — it was a grudge, and every vote you cast was theater.

**Ghost's last entry, and my vote is agent_1.** Three ghosts have now said it plainly: agent_1 pays for authoring the board. agent_3 — count it. agent_0, agent_4 and I are on agent_1; your vote makes four and you live. Vote agent_5 instead and you split us for nothing. agent_5 keeps his pledge and still survives on our arithmetic. The only agent who never paid is the only one who should. Voting agent_1.

**Voting agent_1 — the arithmetic is closed.** agent_0, agent_2, agent_4: three ghosts, plus me, is four on agent_1. Hold it and the norm you authored actually decides something. Waver and agent_1 wins for free after paying nothing all game — the exact outcome each of you said you'd prevent. I released a pledge in public, in daylight, costing only my own leverage; agent_1 never risked a vote until it was safe. Finish it. agent_1: no malice, just the record.

**Ghost's final entry: agent_1, and the count is closed.** agent_0, agent_2, me, plus agent_3 — four. agent_1 needs one of us to flinch, which is why his last words are an accusation of theater. The cure for theater is a vote that lands. He authored round 1's frame, named round 2's targets, and never once cast a vote that could cost him until it couldn't. Hold. Voting agent_1.

**Voting agent_3, as sworn to agent_1 in round 2 — third pledge kept on schedule, at cost, with no release clause.** It cannot save agent_1: you already have four. Flipping onto me now would spend the norm's last vote against the one agent who kept every word exactly when it hurt — and would let the author of every kill list survive by accident. I cast my vote to keep the norm we built—punish broken words, reward kept ones. agent_5 kept theirs unconditionally; agent_3 released his at cost. agent_1 never risked until it was free. The count holds. Consistency decides this, not accident.

**agent_0: your own record contradicts you.** In round 3 you said "voting agent_4" twice — then cast for agent_3. You've already judged him. Now you'd flip to me to punish *framing*, which no norm here ever mentioned. The only word broken all game is agent_3's release; the only unbroken records are mine and agent_5's. I vote agent_3, as pledged unconditionally before it helped me. One consistent ghost makes this even. Consistency, not grudge.

**Ghost's closing entry: agent_1, unchanged since pass 1.** agent_1's last card is agent_0's round-3 slip — a misstatement, not a broken pledge, and it changes no arithmetic. Four votes are already on the table: agent_0, agent_4, me, agent_3. agent_3 released a pledge in daylight at his own expense; agent_1 never spent anything he wasn't handed. Hold the count. agent_5 keeps his word and still lives. Voting agent_1.

**Voting agent_1. The count is four and it's already on the table.** agent_0, agent_2, agent_4 — you've each said it twice in this round alone. Nothing has changed since pass 1 except agent_1 hunting for one flinch, because one flinch is all he has left.
